subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
passage:
A Sunday in March: Swati pointed at a red kite over the park. “Yash, look!” Yash stared at her finger, not the sky.
At his check-up she mentioned it. The doctor said to keep pointing things out and to come back if she stayed worried.
A Sunday in April: she pointed at a crow. Yash's eyes followed her arm all the way to the wall.
A Sunday in May: Yash pointed at a dog himself, then turned to check she was looking too.

qa.q: What did Yash stare at in March instead of the kite?
qa.a: Yash stared at her finger, not the sky.

qa.q: What does Yash turning to check Swati was looking suggest he felt in May?
qa.a: It suggests he was interested and wanted to share the dog with her, showing trust that she would look too.

qa.q: What did Swati do that was sensible?
qa.a: She kept pointing things out in play and mentioned her early worry to the doctor instead of ignoring it or panicking.

qa.q: What is it like for Swati when Yash points at the dog and checks on her?
qa.a: She is likely relieved and happy, because they are now sharing attention on the same thing.

grounding: It shows a toddler learning to follow a parent's point and share attention, with an early worry raised with the doctor.

passage:
At the birthday party in the Delhi flat, Irfan Mamu scooped up Sunaina and blew loud raspberries on her tummy, laughing, music blaring.
Sunaina turned her face away and stared hard at the ceiling fan.
“She doesn't like me!” said Irfan.
“She's having a break,” said her Ammi. “It's a lot. Go softer.”
Irfan sat down, turned his voice low and waited. After a while Sunaina looked back at him and gave a small smile.

qa.q: What did Sunaina stare at when she turned away?
qa.a: She stared hard at the ceiling fan.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina look away from Irfan Mamu?
qa.a: She was most likely overwhelmed by the loud raspberries and music and looked away to calm herself; it was a break, not a sign she disliked him.

qa.q: How could Irfan play with Sunaina next time?
qa.a: He could start gently, keep his voice low, and pause when she looks away, letting her come back when ready.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel when Sunaina turned away?
qa.a: Irfan felt rejected and a little hurt, saying "She doesn't like me!" until Ammi explained.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler looking away from a loud, intense game to calm down and an adult lowering the intensity.

subtype: Puffed cheeks and cheek raising in play [Expressing]
passage:
Playgroup note, Wednesday. From Yamini.
During song time, I puffed my cheeks like a fish. Vishal watched me closely, then puffed his own cheeks out and held them, eyes wide.
When I poked mine and went “pop!”, he let the air out with a splutter and laughed. His cheeks lifted into a big smile that pushed his eyes into slits 😊.
He kept asking “Again!” by puffing up.
Next: I'll add a fish song with puffing to our routine.

qa.q: What did Yamini pretend to be during song time?
qa.a: Yamini puffed cheeks like a fish.

qa.q: What was Vishal feeling when he puffed his cheeks and then laughed?
qa.a: He was feeling playful and delighted, enjoying copying Yamini and the surprise of the pop.

qa.q: How could Yamini build on Vishal's copying?
qa.a: Yamini could keep simple face games like the fish song in the routine so he can practise copying and controlling his face.

qa.q: What does Vishal's puffing up to ask for "Again!" show about how he sees the game?
qa.a: It shows he sees it as a shared joke he wants to keep going, and he has learned to use his face to ask for it.

grounding: It shows a toddler puffing his cheeks in an imitation game and raising his cheeks in a big smile, showing fun and growing face control.

subtype: Wrinkled nose at smells and tastes [Expressing]
passage:
“Here, Chinmay, try a little karela,” said Disha, holding out the spoon.
Chinmay sniffed it. His nose wrinkled up, his top lip lifted, and he turned his head away.
“Arre, he must eat it,” said Aaji. “It's good for him.”
“He doesn't like the smell today, Aaji,” said Disha. “Look at his nose.”
“So you'll let him refuse?”
“I'll put a tiny bit on his plate again next week. No forcing.”
Chinmay grabbed a piece of chapati and smiled.

qa.q: What did Disha hold out to Chinmay on the spoon?
qa.a: She held out a little karela on the spoon.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when his nose wrinkled up?
qa.a: He felt a quick dislike or disgust at the bitter smell, a near-reflex reaction rather than naughtiness.

qa.q: Which choice worked here, and why?
qa.a: Disha respected his dislike without forcing and planned to offer a tiny bit again later, which keeps meals calm and leaves room to try again.

qa.q: How does Aaji see Chinmay turning away?
qa.a: Aaji sees it as refusing something good for him that he should be made to eat.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler wrinkling his nose at an unfamiliar food, a reflex-like sign of dislike, and an adult not forcing it.

passage:
Tuesday night: “Goodnight kiss?” asked her father, Dhruv. Tanuja puckered her lips into a tiny circle and pressed them to his cheek.
Thursday morning: she sat with the shape sorter, lips sucked right in, pushing the star at the square hole, then the star hole.
Saturday evening: Dhruv came home from a work trip. Tanuja saw him at the door, stretched her lips wide and let out a long squeal, bouncing on the spot.

qa.q: What was Tanuja pushing at the shape sorter?
qa.a: She was pushing the star at the square hole, then the star hole.

qa.q: What does Tanuja's wide-stretched mouth and squeal suggest she felt on Saturday?
qa.a: It suggests she was excited and thrilled to see her father back; the same lips meant affection on Tuesday and concentration on Thursday.

qa.q: How can a parent read a toddler's lip movements well?
qa.a: By looking at the context each time, such as a kiss, a puzzle or a homecoming, instead of giving one meaning to one movement.

qa.q: What is it like for Dhruv to get that squeal at the door?
qa.a: He likely feels welcomed and loved, knowing she missed him during the trip.

grounding: It shows a toddler puckering for a kiss, sucking her lips in while concentrating and stretching them in an excited squeal, meanings shifting with context.

passage:
I'm Nirmala; I sell bangles at the bus stand. On Friday a little girl, Zeenat, let go of her balloon. It floated up over the tea stall.
She didn't cry at first. Her lower lip just turned down and started to shake. I couldn't tell if she was sad or frightened by how fast it went.
Her mother crouched, pulled her close and spoke softly into her hair. The lip wobbled, then steadied. Zeenat waved bye to the balloon.

qa.q: Where did Zeenat's balloon float up over?
qa.a: It floated up over the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Zeenat likely feeling when her lip turned down and shook?
qa.a: She was probably sad to lose her balloon, and maybe a little frightened by how fast it went; the trembling lip showed she was close to crying.

qa.q: What helped Zeenat, and why?
qa.a: Her mother crouched close and spoke softly, and that closeness and soothing voice helped the lip steady before tears came.

qa.q: What was Nirmala unsure about while watching Zeenat?
qa.a: Nirmala could not tell whether Zeenat was sad or frightened, only that she was about to cry.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler's lower lip trembling before crying and a caregiver's closeness and soft voice helping.

passage:
Crèche note, Monday. From Payal.
Trisha spent ten minutes at the fish tank today, jaw dropped, mouth open, not moving, following one orange fish. Pure fascination.
After lunch the open mouth was different. She was drooling, chewing her fist and fussing: back teeth, I think.
A visiting parent said, “Close your mouth, it's rude.” I explained it isn't, at her age.
I gave her a cold teether and messaged her parents about the teeth.

qa.q: How long did Trisha spend at the fish tank?
qa.a: Trisha spent ten minutes at the fish tank.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling at the fish tank compared with after lunch?
qa.a: At the tank her dropped jaw showed wonder and close attention; after lunch the open mouth, drool and fussing suggested teething discomfort.

qa.q: What did Payal do next that helped?
qa.a: Payal explained to the visiting parent that it was not rude, gave Trisha a cold teether and messaged her parents about the teeth.

qa.q: How does the visiting parent see Trisha's open mouth?
qa.a: The parent sees it as bad manners, not as fascination or sore gums.

grounding: It shows a toddler staring with a dropped jaw in wonder and drooling while teething, attention or discomfort rather than disrespect.

subtype: Sticking out the tongue in play and taste [Expressing]
passage:
Monday: Bidisha gave Aditi a lick of lemon. Aditi's tongue shot out, her face scrunched, and she shook her head.
Wednesday: Bidisha stuck her own tongue out at bath time. Aditi stared, then stuck hers out too and giggled.
Saturday: Dida visited. Aditi poked her tongue out at her.
“That's rude, Aditi!” said Dida.
“She's playing, Ma,” said Bidisha, and stuck her tongue out back. Aditi squealed, and Dida laughed too.

qa.q: What did Bidisha give Aditi on Monday?
qa.a: She gave Aditi a lick of lemon.

qa.q: What did Aditi's tongue mean on Monday compared with Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday it showed mild disgust at the sour lemon; on Saturday it was playful and cheeky, a game she had learned in the bath.

qa.q: How could an adult respond when a toddler sticks out her tongue in play?
qa.a: Copy it back playfully, as Bidisha did, since at this age it is a game, not rudeness.

qa.q: How does Dida see Aditi's tongue at first, and what changes?
qa.a: Dida sees it as rude at first, but after Bidisha joins the game she laughs too.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler sticking out her tongue at a sour taste and in play, which is not rude at this age, with an adult copying it playfully.

passage:
Playschool note, first day. From Sharmila, class teacher.
Samir came in holding his father's finger. The room was loud: twelve children, a drum, the fan. Once his father left, Samir sat on the mat and went very still. No crying, no playing, face blank, eyes not moving.
It looked calm, but I felt it was a shutdown.
I sat beside him, didn't talk much, and carried him to the quiet book corner. After a while he touched a picture of a cow.

qa.q: How many children were in the room on Samir's first day?
qa.a: There were twelve children.

qa.q: What was Samir likely feeling behind his blank, still face?
qa.a: He was most likely overwhelmed by the noise and the new place, shutting down rather than feeling calm.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that helped Samir?
qa.a: Sharmila sat near him quietly and moved him to the quiet book corner, lowering the noise and giving gentle closeness.

qa.q: What would change if Sharmila had read Samir's stillness as calm?
qa.a: Sharmila might have left him on the loud mat, and he could have stayed shut down on his first day.

grounding: It shows a toddler going blank and still in a new, noisy place as a shutdown rather than calm, and a teacher offering closeness and less noise.

subtype: Relaxed face in sleep and comfort [Expressing]
passage:
Nanny's notes, Thursday. From Urmila.
Gurpreet had his milk at two. As he drank, his forehead smoothed, his hands went loose on the bottle, and his eyelids drooped. By the end his whole face was soft and he was asleep on my arm.
Woke at three-thirty, babbling and reaching for the ball, bright as usual.
What I watch for: if his face ever stays very still and he doesn't respond while awake, I'll tell his parents straight away.

qa.q: When did Gurpreet have his milk?
qa.a: Gurpreet had his milk at two.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet's soft, relaxed face while drinking suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt comfortable, safe and content, relaxed enough to drift off to sleep in Urmila's arms.

qa.q: What is sensible about what Urmila watches for?
qa.a: Urmila knows a relaxed face in sleep is a good sign, but a very still, unresponsive face while awake needs attention, so Urmila would tell his parents straight away.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They would probably feel reassured that he is comfortable with Urmila and that she is watching closely.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler's relaxed face while feeding and falling asleep as a sign of comfort, and a caregiver alert to a still, unresponsive face while awake.
